claims.claim: Medically recognised incontinence was linked with higher adjusted risk of nursing home admission.
claims.supporting_passage: The adjusted risk of admission to a nursing facility was 2.0 times greater for incontinent women (95% CI = 1.7-2.4) and 3.2 times greater for incontinent men (95% CI = 2.7-3.8).
claims.pico_timeframe: 5,986 HMO members 65+, California / medically recognised UI / none / nursing home admission / follow-up period not stated in abstract
claims.safe_wording: In an older US study of about 6,000 people aged 65 and over, those whose incontinence was recorded by doctors were about twice (women) and three times (men) as likely to move into a nursing home, after allowing for age and other illnesses. This shows a link, not that treating incontinence prevents a move.
claims.qualifications: Association from a 1990s US cohort; relative risks; no timing-of-decision language (editor).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Authors' conclusion uses causal 'increases'; do not repeat.

claims.claim: Family carers of people with dementia often do not seek professional help with incontinence until a crisis, and find product access inconsistent.
claims.supporting_passage: Most carers reported protecting the person's dignity by not seeking health professionals help often until the point of a crisis. ... carers report local health service policies on access to continence products to be inconsistent and often inappropriate to their circumstances.
claims.safe_wording: In a UK interview study of 32 family carers of people with dementia, most said they held off asking professionals for help with incontinence, often until a crisis.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: 'Harder than behavioural symptoms' comes from the paper's background citations; not verified; drop.

claims.claim: Clinicians should ask about continence, and assessment should be comprehensive and multidisciplinary.
claims.supporting_passage: As a minimum, clinicians should actively ask patients about continence, especially in older adults living with frailty. Careful evaluation and establishment of any underpinning diagnosis and aetiological factors requires comprehensive, multimodal, usually multidisciplinary, assessment.
claims.safe_wording: Specialists in older people's care advise that clinicians ask about continence and that assessment looks for causes, usually with more than one professional.
claims.qualifications: Expert review, not a formal guideline.

claims.claim: Medicines, extra urine output, difficulty getting to the toilet and constipation can contribute to incontinence in older people.
claims.supporting_passage: Other causes do not directly affect the urinary system but are related to difficulties in reacting to the urge to urinate or getting to the toilet alone, or an increase in urine output. ... Drugs known to cause urinary incontinence are often prescribed for older patients ...: sedatives, neuroleptics, antidepressants, cholinesterase inhibitors used in Alzheimer's disease, diuretics, alpha blockers ... | Among older patients the effects of decreased cognition and impaired mobility can be substantial, and environmental barriers can play a role. When managing older patients with UI, emphasis on treating concurrent conditions, optimizing medications, and working on lifestyle and behavioural factors is at least as important as pharmacologic treatment. | Fewer patients reported urgency (16 versus 34, p < 0.001), frequency (25 versus 47, p < 0.001)
claims.pico_timeframe: Older people / reviews; Charach: 52 people 65-89 before-after
claims.safe_wording: Some contributors can be looked for and changed: medicines such as water tablets and sedatives, difficulty getting to the toilet, and constipation. In one small study, treating constipation in older people was followed by less urgency and frequency.
claims.qualifications: Constipation evidence is a small uncontrolled study of bladder symptoms, not incontinence.

claims.claim: Trial evidence for continence treatments delivered at home, especially in dementia, is limited.
claims.supporting_passage: Two studies focusing on multicomponent behavioural interventions showed benefit ... Three, which included cognitively impaired people, reported improvement with toileting assistance programmes, but the effects were not all significant. ... There is scant evidence for continence supporting interventions delivered in older people's own homes. | There was insufficient evidence from any studies to recommend any strategies.
claims.pico_timeframe: Homebound older people; people with dementia at home
claims.safe_wording: Research on help at home is thin: a 2024 review found only seven trials, and a review in dementia found too little evidence to recommend any approach. Assessment may still find something that helps; it may not.
claims.qualifications: Must be stated so the post does not promise results.

claims.claim: Incontinence can arise from difficulty reaching or using the toilet (mobility, cognition, environment).
claims.supporting_passage: Other causes do not directly affect the urinary system but are related to difficulties in reacting to the urge to urinate or getting to the toilet alone ... | Among older patients the effects of decreased cognition and impaired mobility can be substantial, and environmental barriers can play a role.
claims.safe_wording: Some leaks happen because getting to the toilet, or using it, is hard: slow walking, memory problems, or the route and room itself.
claims.qualifications: Not quantified; do not say 'often one broken link'.

claims.claim: Weekly urge incontinence linked with falls and fractures in older women.
claims.supporting_passage: weekly or more frequent urge incontinence was associated independently with risk of falling (odds ratio = 1.26; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.14-1.40) and with non-spine nontraumatic fracture (relative hazard 1.34 ...). Stress incontinence was not associated independently with falls or fracture.
claims.pico_timeframe: 6,049 US women mean 78.5 / weekly urge UI / none / falls, fractures / ~3 years
claims.safe_wording: In a US study of about 6,000 older women, leaking with urgency at least weekly was linked with more falls and fractures over three years; leaking on coughing was not. Rushing to the toilet is one suggested explanation, not proven.
claims.qualifications: Association; odds ratio not to be turned into 'times'.

claims.claim: Night-time toilet trips (nocturia) are linked with falls.
claims.supporting_passage: Nocturia is probably associated with an approximately 1.2-fold increased risk of falls ... We rated the quality of evidence for nocturia as a prognostic factor as moderate for falls ... and as very low as a cause of falls/fractures.
claims.safe_wording: Getting up at night to pass urine is linked with a somewhat higher risk of falls; whether it causes falls is uncertain.

claims.claim: Changing the route or environment (lighting, commode, clothing) improves continence.
claims.supporting_passage: environmental barriers can play a role.
claims.safe_wording: Present chair height, clear lit route, commode or bottle and easy clothing as practical things to check, not as trial-proven treatments.
claims.qualifications: No trial evidence found for individual adaptations.

claims.claim: 41% of screened incontinent residents responded to prompted voiding; wet checks fell 26.7% to 6.4% and 9.6% at 9 weeks.
claims.supporting_passage: A cohort of 191 incontinent, long-stay nursing home residents who passed a simple behavioral screen (able to state their name or reliably point to one of two named objects). ... Seventy-eight (41%) of the residents were responders. Their wet percentage went from 26.7% to 6.4% at the end of 1 week and was maintained at 9.6% after 9 weeks of prompted voiding.
claims.pico_timeframe: 191 US residents passing screen / PV 7am-7pm by research aides / baseline / % hourly checks wet / 1 and 9 weeks
claims.safe_wording: In seven US nursing homes in the 1990s, about 4 in 10 residents who could follow a simple instruction became mostly dry in the day with regular prompts; in them, wet checks fell from about 1 in 4 to about 1 in 16 and stayed near 1 in 10 at nine weeks.
claims.qualifications: 4 in 10 of those who passed the screen, not all screened; research aides delivered prompts; daytime only.

claims.claim: A 3-day trial identifies likely responders.
claims.supporting_passage: The best sensitivity and specificity in identifying responders was achieved when either the wet percentage was lower than 20% or the appropriate toileting percentage was higher than 66% during the first 3 days of prompted voiding (sensitivity, 87%; specificity, 69%).
claims.safe_wording: A three-day trial picked out most people who went on to respond, though not perfectly.
claims.qualifications: Framing new residents' first weeks is the post's suggestion.

claims.claim: Cochrane: short-term benefit of prompted voiding.
claims.supporting_passage: The limited evidence suggested that prompted voiding increased self-initiated voiding and decreased incontinent episodes in the short-term. There was no evidence about long-term effects.
claims.safe_wording: A review of five small trials found suggestive short-term benefit, with no evidence on the long term.

claims.claim: Night-time prompted voiding not effective for most.
claims.supporting_passage: nighttime PV ... was not an effective intervention ... routine nighttime toileting programs should not be carried out for the majority of incontinent NH residents. Instead, individualized care based on resident's preferences, willingness to toilet at night, and sleep patterns should be emphasized.
claims.safe_wording: At night, waking residents for the toilet did not work for most; plan nights around the person's sleep and wishes.

claims.claim: Prompted voiding needs staff time.
claims.supporting_passage: Both interventions had labor costs that were greater than "usual care" costs. | inadequate staffing, workload, and turnover/absenteeism hindered implementation.
claims.safe_wording: Prompting takes more care-worker time than usual care, and staff report short staffing as the main barrier.

claims.claim: Burgio trial results.
claims.supporting_passage: Behavioral treatment, which yielded a mean 80.7% reduction of incontinence episodes, was significantly more effective than drug treatment (mean 68.5% reduction; P=.04) and both were more effective than the placebo control condition (mean 39.4% reduction ...). Only 14.0% of patients receiving behavioral treatment wanted to change to another treatment vs 75.5% in each of the other groups. ... Subjects had to have urodynamic evidence of bladder dysfunction, be ambulatory, and not have dementia.
claims.pico_timeframe: 197 women 55-92 / 8 weeks behavioural (4 sessions) vs oxybutynin vs placebo / leaks by diary
claims.safe_wording: In a US trial of 197 women aged 55 to 92 who walked unaided and did not have dementia, eight weeks of behavioural treatment with biofeedback cut leaks by about 81% on average, oxybutynin by about 69% and a dummy pill by about 39%. About 1 in 7 on behavioural treatment wanted to switch, against 3 in 4 in the other groups.
claims.qualifications: Call it behavioural treatment with pelvic floor training and urge control, not 'bladder training'; single trial.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Cochrane 2012 (C12-20-c) found drugs beat bladder training alone in small trials.

claims.claim: Behavioural training (Burgio) includes pelvic floor training and urge suppression, distinct from bladder training.
claims.supporting_passage: Multicomponent behavioral training is another form of behavioral treatment that includes pelvic floor muscle training and exercise. ... Using biofeedback or other teaching methods, patients learn strategies to inhibit bladder contraction using pelvic floor muscle contraction and other urge suppression strategies. ... few patients are cured with either treatment alone.
claims.safe_wording: The behavioural treatment taught women to squeeze pelvic floor muscles and other ways to hold off the urge.

claims.claim: Conflicting: drugs vs bladder training.
claims.supporting_passage: During treatment, symptomatic improvement was more common amongst those participants on anticholinergic drugs compared with bladder training in seven small trials (73/174, 42% versus 98/172, 57% not improved ...).
claims.safe_wording: Across seven small trials, bladder training alone did less well than bladder tablets; the post must say this.

claims.claim: Guidelines recommend bladder training first, drugs if unsuccessful.
claims.supporting_passage: ACP recommends bladder training in women with urgency UI. ... ACP recommends pharmacologic treatment in women with urgency UI if bladder training was unsuccessful.
claims.safe_wording: A US physicians' guideline recommends bladder training first for urge leaking in women, with tablets if it does not work.
claims.qualifications: NICE NG123 not opened; do not cite NICE.

claims.claim: Persistence with antimuscarinics at 12 months 14% to 35%.
claims.supporting_passage: At 12 months, the proportions of patients still on their original treatment were: solifenacin 35% ... flavoxate 14%.
claims.safe_wording: In UK prescription records, between about 1 in 7 and 1 in 3 people were still on their first bladder tablet a year later.

numbers.meaning: still on original drug at 12 months

claims.claim: GROUP trial results.
claims.supporting_passage: Median percentage reduction in urinary incontinence episodes was 70% (95% CI, 44%-89%) in individual PFMT compared with 74% (95% CI, 46%-86%) in group-based PFMT ... confirming noninferiority.
claims.pico_timeframe: 362 Canadian women 60+ / group of 8 vs individual, 12 weeks / leaks at 1 year
claims.safe_wording: In a Canadian trial of 362 women aged 60 and over, weekly classes of eight reduced leaks about as much as one-to-one sessions at one year: typical reductions about 3 in 4 and 7 in 10.

claims.claim: Individual session first; physiotherapist-led; exclusions.
claims.supporting_passage: After an individual session with a physiotherapist to learn how to effectively contract the pelvic floor muscle (PFM), women in both treatment arms received a 12-week PFMT program under the direction of an experienced pelvic floor physiotherapist ... Exclusion criteria were body mass index (BMI) 35 or greater ..., reduced mobility (requiring a mobility aid), chronic constipation
claims.safe_wording: Every woman had one individual session first; classes were led by experienced physiotherapists; women needing a walking aid were excluded.

claims.claim: Clinically important reduction by week 4.
claims.supporting_passage: Median minimal and incremental clinically important differences were achieved by the 4th and 6th weeks of treatment. ... Age, UI duration, severity, pelvic floor strength, and group-based intervention were related to later treatment response.
claims.safe_wording: Half of women had halved their leaks by about week 4; group classes tended to take a little longer.

claims.claim: Guidelines recommend supervised PFMT first-line.
claims.supporting_passage: ACP recommends first-line treatment with pelvic floor muscle training in women with stress UI. | National and international clinical practice guidelines recommend supervised individual PFMT as first-line treatment for women with stress or mixed urinary incontinence.
claims.safe_wording: Guidelines recommend supervised pelvic floor training as the first treatment for stress or mixed leaking.
claims.qualifications: Do not cite NICE specifics (not opened).

candidates.reason: Thom association, carer delay, assessment advice, modifiable contributors and limited home-treatment evidence all supported; 'harder than behavioural symptoms' dropped.
Definition and falls links supported; 'one broken link' and adaptations are unquantified/not trial-tested.
candidates.revised_angle: Present the chain as a practical checklist (judgement), with sourced statement that mobility, memory and environment contribute; add night version with nocturia-falls link as association.

candidates.reason: All figures verified; state 'of those who passed a screen', research staff, staff time, night limits.
Burgio supported but Cochrane 2012 conflicts; NICE not opened.
candidates.revised_angle: Weighing it up: behavioural treatment with pelvic floor/urge training outperformed oxybutynin in one trial of older women without dementia; bladder training alone did less well than tablets in pooled small trials; guideline (ACP) says try bladder training first, tablets if it fails; many stop tablets within a year.

candidates.reason: Full text verified; noninferiority wording; exclusions and physiotherapist-led stated; NICE replaced by ACP/Dumoulin.
